intro: Reporting a question needs two more changes than reporting a statement: the word order becomes the order of a statement, and the auxiliary do / does / did disappears. “Where do you live?” becomes “She asked me where I lived.” We also report requests and orders with ask / tell + someone + to.
objectifs: Report a wh- question with asked + question word + subject + verb (no inversion, no do).
Report a yes/no question with if or whether.
Apply the tense, pronoun and time-word changes from lesson 104.
Report a request or an order with ask / tell + person + (not) to + verb.

texte: Keep the question word (what, where, when, why, how, who, which, how much…), then use statement word order: subject + verb. There is no question mark.
The auxiliary do / does / did disappears, and the main verb takes the backshifted tense: “Where do you work?” → “He asked me where I worked.” “What did you buy?” → “She asked me what I had bought.”
The most common reporting verbs are ask, want to know and wonder. Ask can be followed by a person (asked me) or not (asked).

lignes: She asked me where I lived.
He asked me what I was doing.
They asked her why she had left.
I asked how much it cost.
She wanted to know when I would arrive.
He asked who had taken his pen.

texte: For a question that has a yes or no answer, use if or whether, then statement word order. “Are you hungry?” → “She asked me if I was hungry.”
Whether is a little more formal and is used especially when there are two options: “He asked whether I wanted tea or coffee.” We also say “whether or not”.
exemples: “Do you speak French?” → She asked me if I spoke French.
“Have you seen my keys?” → He asked if I had seen his keys.
“Can you help me?” → She asked me whether I could help her.
“Is it raining?” → He wanted to know if it was raining.

texte: All the rules from lesson 104 apply: tenses move back after a past reporting verb, and pronouns, possessives, and time and place words change (tomorrow → the next day, here → there).
If the reporting verb is in the present (He asks / wants to know), there is no backshift: “The customer wants to know when the parcel will arrive.”
exemples: “Will you come to my party tomorrow?” → She asked me if I would come to her party the next day.
will → would; my → her; tomorrow → the next day.
“What time does this shop close?” → The tourist wants to know what time this shop closes.

sections.titre: Requests and orders: ask / tell + to
texte: To report a polite request (Could you…? Please…), use ask + person + to + verb. To report an order or instruction (imperative), use tell + person + to + verb.
In the negative, not goes before to: “Don't be late” → “She told me not to be late.” Not “She told me don't be late”. (“to not be late” is heard in speech, but avoid it in careful English.)

lignes: She asked me to open the window.
The teacher told us to sit down.
He asked us not to smoke there.
My mother told me not to touch it.

exemples: My boss asked me to send the report before Friday.
The police officer told the driver not to move.

texte: The same structure (question word + subject + verb) is used in polite indirect questions in the present: “Could you tell me where the station is?”, “Do you know what time it starts?”. This is the topic of lesson 114.
The trap is the same in both cases: keeping the inversion of the direct question. “Can you tell me where is the station?” is wrong.
exemples: Do you know where the post office is?

formule: asked (+ person) + wh- / if / whether + subject + verb (tense moved back) · asked / told + person + (not) to + verb
prononciation: asked /ɑːskt/ (US /æskt/): three consonants at the end, s-k-t. Don't say “ask”: the -ed /t/ must be heard.
A reported question doesn't have question intonation: the voice falls at the end, like a statement. “She asked me where I LIVED ↘.”
In “told me not to”, the stress falls on not: “She told me NOT to wait.”
erreurs: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
No did and no inversion in a reported question.
He asked me where was the station.
He asked me where the station was.
Statement order: subject + verb.
She asked me do I like coffee.
She asked me if I liked coffee.
Yes/no question: if / whether.
He asked me what time is it.
He asked me what time it was.
Statement order and backshift.
She asked if I was hungry?
She asked if I was hungry.
No question mark.
He told me don't call him.
He told me not to call him.
Negative order: told + person + not to.
She said me to wait.
She told me to wait. / She asked me to wait.
Don't use say + person + to for orders: use tell or ask.

dialogue.contexte: Brussels, after a job interview. Olivier tells his flatmate Emmanuel, from Kinshasa, about the questions he was asked.
lignes: So, what did they ask you?
First, they asked me why I wanted to work for them.
The manager asked me if I had ever managed a team, and how many people I had worked with.
If + past perfect; how many + subject + verb.
Did they ask whether you spoke Dutch?
Yes! And they wanted to know when I could start.
At the end, they asked me to send them two references and told me not to worry about the test.

mots: She asked me where I lived.
to say or write a question
He wanted to know how much it cost.
They asked whether I was free on Monday.
A customer enquired whether the shop was open.
to ask for information (formal; US: inquire)
The officer ordered them to stop.
to tell someone to do something, with authority
She reminded me to buy bread.
They asked me to send two references.
a letter or contact from someone who knows your work

exercices.consigne: Choose the correct reported question (a or b).
items: “Where are you going?” a) She asked me where was I going. b) She asked me where I was going.
b
“Do you like jazz?” a) He asked if I liked jazz. b) He asked did I like jazz.
a
“What time is it?” a) I asked what time it was. b) I asked what time was it.
a
“Don't shout!” a) She told us to not shouting. b) She told us not to shout.
b

exercices.consigne: Report the question, starting with “She asked me…”.
items: “Where do you work?”
She asked me where I worked.
“What are you reading?”
She asked me what I was reading.
“Why did you call?”
She asked me why I had called.
“How long will you stay?”
She asked me how long I would stay.
“Who is your teacher?”
She asked me who my teacher was.

exercices.consigne: Report the question with if or whether, starting with “He asked (me)…”.
items: “Are you married?”
He asked me if (whether) I was married.
“Can you drive?”
He asked me if (whether) I could drive.
“Have you finished the report?”
He asked me if (whether) I had finished the report.
“Do you want tea or coffee?”
He asked me whether I wanted tea or coffee.

exercices.consigne: Report with asked / told + person + (not) to.
items: The doctor to me: “Stay in bed.”
The doctor told me to stay in bed.
My friend to me: “Could you lend me your car?”
My friend asked me to lend him (her) my car.
The guide to the tourists: “Don't take photos.”
The guide told the tourists not to take photos.
My neighbour to us: “Please don't make noise after ten.”
My neighbour asked us not to make noise after ten.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: She asked me where did I buy my shoes.
She asked me where I had bought my shoes. / She asked me where I bought my shoes.
They asked us were we tired.
They asked us if (whether) we were tired.
He told me don't be late.
He told me not to be late.
I asked her how old is she.
I asked her how old she was.

exercices.consigne: Think of an interview, a doctor's appointment or a first meeting. In 4–5 sentences, report the questions you were asked, and one request or order.
items: Example answer

Last week I went to the doctor's. She asked me how long I had had the cough. She wanted to know if I smoked and whether I was taking any medicine. Then she asked me to breathe deeply. At the end, she told me to drink a lot of water and not to go to work for two days.

a_retenir: Reported wh- question: asked + question word + subject + verb (no do, no inversion).
Yes/no question: asked + if / whether + subject + verb.
Backshift and pronoun changes as for statements.
No question mark and no rising intonation.
Request: asked + person + to; order: told + person + to; negative: not to.
